### Questions

This is a metadata export from the Library of Congress, covering 500 color photographs
taken between 1939 and 1943 for the Farm Security Administration and the Office of War
Information. The FSA sent photographers out to document rural poverty during the
Depression; after Pearl Harbor the same unit photographed aircraft plants and rail
yards instead.

A row is one photograph. The columns are a `filepath` pointing at the image file, a
`call_number` (the archive's catalogue id), the `photographer`, a `caption`, the `year`
and `month` it was taken, the `state`, `city`, and `county`, and a `longitude` and
`latitude`.

The file was messy enough that the setup code needed several extra arguments just to
read it. Nobody wrote down what was wrong with it, and today we work out what its data
dictionary should have said.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it
to a variable.

1. Start with a warm-up. Count the photographs taken by each `photographer` and sort
from the most to the fewest.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .group_by(c.photographer)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

Jack Delano took 162 of the 500 photographs.

2. Count the photographs taken in each `year`, sort by year, and draw the result with
`geom_col`.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .group_by(c.year)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.year)
    .ggplot(aes(c.year, c.n))
    .geom_col()
)
```

3. The chapter gives two ways to record a date: one column for each part, or a single
`YYYY-MM-DD` string. This file uses separate `year` and `month` columns. Count the
photographs in each year and month, sorted by the count from largest to smallest.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .group_by(c.year, c.month)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

The archive knows the month of each photograph but not the day, so separate columns
are the only honest choice. A `YYYY-MM-DD` date would have needed a made-up day.

4. Take the code from the previous question and draw a line plot of the count over
time. To get a single date for the x-axis, add a column `date` equal to
`pl.date(c.year, c.month, 1)` and sort by it.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .group_by(c.year, c.month)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .with_columns(date = pl.date(c.year, c.month, 1))
    .sort(c.date)
    .ggplot(aes(c.date, c.n))
    .geom_line()
)
```

Putting every photograph on the first of the month is fine for a plot. It would not
be fine in the data file itself.

5. The `call_number` should identify each photograph. Count the rows for each
`call_number` and sort from the most rows to the fewest.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .group_by(c.call_number)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

One call number, `LC-DIG-fsac-1a35424`, appears twice.

6. Filter to the rows whose `filepath` contains the text `"1a3543"`, sort by
`filepath`, and select the columns `filepath` and `call_number`.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .filter(c.filepath.str.contains("1a3543"))
    .sort(c.filepath)
    .select(c.filepath, c.call_number)
)
```

Every call number matches its file name digit for digit, except for the duplicated
row: the file `1a35434v.jpg` carries the call number `...1a35424`. The row was entered
twice and two digits of the call number were swapped. Because the file name is also
stored in the table, as the chapter suggests for images, we can tell which column is
wrong.

7. The chapter says to leave a missing value blank. Count the missing values in each
column with `.null_count()`.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .null_count()
)
```

There are no missing values at all, which is surprising for a file of 500 photographs
from 1939.

8. Filter to the photographs taken in the `"District of Columbia"` and select the
columns `city` and `county`.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .filter(c.state == "District of Columbia")
    .select(c.city, c.county)
)
```

Washington, DC is not in any county, so these five values should be missing. Instead
the file has a code, `US.DC.001`, sitting in a column of county names. A data
dictionary is where a value like this has to be explained.

9. Filter to the photographs taken in `"California"`, then count them by `county` and
`city`.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .filter(c.state == "California")
    .group_by(c.county, c.city)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

There is no "Los County" or "San County" in California. Every value in this column has
been cut down to two words, so Los Angeles County and San Bernardino County lost a
word. A standard code, such as the county's FIPS number, could not have been damaged
this way.

10. Draw a map of the photographs, with `longitude` on the x-axis and `latitude` on
the y-axis, colored by `year`.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .ggplot(aes(c.longitude, c.latitude))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.year))
)
```

11. Group by `state` and `city` and compute the number of photographs and the number of
distinct longitudes with `c.longitude.n_unique()`. Sort by the number of photographs.

```{python}
(
    photos
    .group_by(c.state, c.city)
    .agg(
        n = pl.len(),
        n_lon = c.longitude.n_unique()
    )
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
```

Every city has exactly one longitude, no matter how many photographs were taken there.
The coordinates are the center of the town, not the place where the camera stood, so
the map in the previous question is a map of towns.

12. Last question, and it is a written one. Write the data dictionary this file should
have come with. For each column, give what it holds, its type, and anything a reader
needs to know about it.

**Answer**: `filepath` (string) is the image file, relative to the archive's media
folder. `call_number` (string) is the catalogue id and the primary key, except that one
photograph was entered twice with a typo (`1a35424` should be `1a35434`).
`photographer` (string) is the photographer's name. `caption` (string) was written by
the archive. `year` and `month` (integers) are the date taken; the day is not known.
`state` (string) is the full state name and `city` (string) is the town.
`county` (string) is cut down to two words, so names such as Los Angeles County are
wrong, and Washington, DC uses the code `US.DC.001` in place of a missing value.
`longitude` and `latitude` (numbers) are the center of the city, not the location of
the photograph.
